title: Part 1
text: If this parasite is old, why did the 1990s bring such a startling wave of deformed frogs? This is where humans re-enter the story.

title: Part 2
text: Pieter Johnson and his colleagues found a link between nutrient pollution and the severity of these infections.
nxt: Farmers use large amounts of fertilizer containing nitrogen and phosphorus to boost crop yields.

title: Part 3
text: First, the nutrients feed blooms of green algae that blanket the pond in thick green sludge.
nxt: For ramshorn snails, that algae is an all-you-can-eat buffet. Snail populations in nutrient-rich ponds can grow sharply.

title: Part 4
text: More snails means more homes for Ribeiroia. Ordinary ponds can turn into parasite-breeding superfactories.
nxt: A study published in 2007 found that nutrient enrichment raised snail numbers, and those snails then released more infectious parasites into the water.

title: Part 5
text: In a balanced pond, a tadpole might meet only a few cercariae, and the effects may be minor.
nxt: In a nutrient-rich pond, a tadpole can be attacked by many parasites at once. Its developing body is overwhelmed by the sheer number of invaders.

title: Part 6
text: It is worth being honest about the limits of this story. Ribeiroia explains the multi-legged frogs, but it is not the only threat amphibians face.
nxt: Habitat loss, disease, and other factors also harm frogs around the world, and not every deformity in every pond has the same cause.

title: Part 7
text: Think of how many links had to line up: rain, fertilizer, algae, snails, parasites, tadpoles, birds. Push too hard on one link and the whole pond can tip over.
nxt: It also shows why the first answer, a toxic spill, felt so natural. People look for a single villain.
